title: Effects of media representations of drug related deaths on public stigma and support for harm reduction

claims.statement: In one randomized online experiment with UK adults, details in a simulated news report of a drug death changed how much stigma readers said they felt towards the person who died, by small to moderate amounts, but hardly changed their stated support for harm-reduction policies. In June 2022, 1,248 adults on a UK online research panel (Prolific; mean age 45.7, 51.0% women) were each randomly assigned to read one of eight versions of a BBC-style news story about an inquest, adapted from a real 2019 report of an ecstasy death; the versions differed in the person's gender (Jane or John), age together with use history (21 and had used the drug 'once or twice', or 43 and had used it regularly for 15 years) and drug (ecstasy or heroin). Stigma towards the person, on a new nine-item measure of blame, anger, pity, responsibility, control and wish for distance (range 9 to 81), was higher when the person was a man (mean 45.6 against 43.4 for a woman), when the person was older with long use (46.7 against 42.3) and when the drug was heroin (46.9 against 42.1): about 0.2, 0.4 and 0.4 standard deviations (editors' calculation), with the eight versions ranging from 38.6 (young woman, ecstasy) to 50.1 (older man, heroin). Support for six harm-reduction policies (such as drug checking, drug consumption rooms, take-home naloxone and opioid agonist treatment; range 6 to 30) was slightly higher after the older person's story (about 23.6 against 23.0, editors' calculation from the condition means, about 0.1 standard deviation; the paper prints the two means in reverse order), a difference seen in the ecstasy stories only, and did not differ by drug or by gender. In exploratory, non-randomized analyses of 868 participants, stronger belief in a just world, less perspective-taking and more general stigma towards people with drug problems went with more stigma towards the person, and having seen media coverage of a family affected by a drug death went with less (Sumnall et al., 2023). The study was not registered in advance, the stigma measure was new, the panel was matched to the UK population on sex, age and ethnicity only and over-represented people with degrees and people who prefer left-wing parties, the outcomes were self-reports measured once straight after one written story, and 'older' cannot be separated from 'longer use'. How real news coverage affects behaviour, policy or the people affected was not studied. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Sumnall et al. (2023), 2 × 2 × 2 factorial, n = 1,248 (degrees of freedom imply 1,238 analysed). Stigma (9–81): man 45.6 (SD 12.1) against woman 43.4 (12.6), F(1,1230) = 11.1, p < .001; older with 15 years' use 46.7 (11.8) against younger first-time 42.3 (12.7), F = 40.5, p < .001; heroin 46.9 (11.5) against ecstasy 42.1 (12.8), F = 50.1, p < .001; editors' d about 0.18, 0.36 and 0.39; condition means 38.6 to 50.1. Harm-reduction support (6–30): age, F = 4.5, p = .035 (older about 23.6 against younger 23.0, editors' calculation; d about 0.12); within ecstasy stories, F = 4.8, p = .029 (about 23.9 against 22.7); gender F = .0, p = .802; drug F = .0, p = .922. Exploratory regression (868 participants, editors' calculation from degrees of freedom): story factors R² = .068, final model R² = .569.
